newsitem.title: IRAQ: UN oil inspectors travel to northern Iraq.
newsitem.headline: UN oil inspectors travel to northern Iraq.

text.p: Three international oil experts left Baghdad for northern Iraq on Tuesday to inspect the country's oil facilities for possible implementation of a delayed oil-for-food deal with the United Nations.

Wolde Ammar, spokesman for Iraq's U.N. coordinator, said the experts ended on Monday a three-day inspection of Iraq's southern Mina al-Bakr oil terminal, checking its metering equipment and facilities to see whether they can handle oil exports.
The terminal, with a total export capactiy of more than one million barrels per day (bpd), sustained heavy damage during the 1991 Gulf War. The Iraqis say they have repaired the facility.

"They (experts) are a fact finding mission...They are travelling to the north today (Tuesday). They will go to Beiji oil complex (135 miles north of Baghdad) and then they proceed to Zakho tracing the Iraqi-Turkish oil pipeline," Ammar told Reuters.
The deal allows Iraq exports worth $2 billion over six months to raise money for food and medical supplies to alleviate the effects of U.N. sanctions imposed after its 1990 invasion of Kuwait.

Part of the experts' mission, according to Ammar, is to check the gauging tools at Iraq's export outlets and see whehter they are fit to measure the quality and quantity of Iraqi crude exports under the oil-for-food plan.
The experts also met officials from Iraq's oil ministry who guided them on their tour of southern Iraq.

Iraq intends to export 450,000 bpd via Turkey out of an estimated 700,000-800,000 bpd it would be allowed to pump to the outside world at current prices. The remainder is planned to be exported through terminals in the Gulf.

The deal, signed in May, is still on hold because of securiy concerns in northern Iraq sparked by Baghdad's dispatch of troops in August to help a Kurdish faction fighting a rival. A U.S.-brokered ceasefire last week halted the inter-Kurdish fighting.
U.N. aid agencies on Monday expressed alarm at the lack of food, medicine and clean water in Iraq, estimating that 4,500 children were dying monthly, in part because of the stringent trade sanctions.

U.N. sources in New York said that the U.S. was still to approve the oil pricing formula, already endorsed by other Security Council members. They also said differences on number of U.N. food distribution monitors and freedom of their movement still remained unresolved.
